items.title: GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.117 fixes MCP approval leakage
facts: Approving an MCP server's tools for the session or for a location no longer also approves Copilot's built-in requests, such as shell commands or memory stores, when the server's name matches a built-in permission type.
The approval still covers that server's tools, including after the session is resumed.
Added sandbox.userPolicy.network.extraCaCertificates to trust custom CA certificates for sandboxed commands through TLS-intercepting proxies.

x_posts.author: @fernandogomes
x_posts.text:
GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.117 came out this morning with a permission fix worth knowing about.

Before it, approving an MCP server's tools for the session or for a location could also approve Copilot's own built-in requests, like shell commands or memory stores, when the server's name matched a built-in permission type. Now the approval covers only that server's tools.

When you approve an MCP server for a whole session, do you know exactly what that approval covers?

x_posts.author: @thomas_rehmer
x_posts.text:
GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.117, the AI coding agent that works in your terminal, changes how far a single yes from you reaches.

Until now, allowing the tools of an MCP server (an add-on that gives the agent extra tools) also allowed shell commands (commands that run directly on your computer), when the add-on's name matched one of Copilot's built-in permission types.

Now that yes covers the add-on's own tools, also when you pick the session up again, and no longer Copilot's built-in requests.

Think of an add-on that happens to share its name with a built-in permission: allowing it no longer lets the agent run shell commands as well.

A yes now belongs to the add-on it was given for, not to a name that happens to match.

https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/releases/tag/v1.0.117

items.title: Antigravity CLI 1.5.18 resolves file:/// permission gaps and image handling
facts: Fixed the agent attaching truncated or corrupt images to the conversation when viewing files; it now rejects them with an error, so a half-written image no longer makes later model requests fail and retry.
Fixed file permission rules and approval prompts not applying to files the agent reads or edits through file:/// URIs; those paths now resolve to the real file before permissions are checked.
Fixed plugins not loading on Windows when your workspace is on a different drive than your Antigravity configuration directory.

items.title: OpenCode 2.4.2 limits Always allow web fetches and adds GPT-6.2 prompts
facts: "Always allow" for a web fetch allows that site only. It used to allow every URL.
GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra, and the gpt-latest aliases, use a system prompt written for GPT-6.2.
generate_image and generate_video run inside Code Mode instead of as top-level tools, so their definitions no longer add about 700 tokens to every request.

items.title: enhance-qa brings independent QA teams inside coding agents
facts: A scout maps every screen and control and writes the test checklist.
Only the fixer touches your code. Nobody grades their own work.
Works with Claude Code and Codex, plus Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and Antigravity.

x_posts.author: @rohanvijaykumar
x_posts.text:
Your coding agent is grading its own homework.

It writes the feature, tests it, fixes what fails, then tells you it's ready to ship. Of course it passes.

I started in QA, testing DVD and Blu-ray menus. Every disc went through the same cycle: a smoke test when a build arrived, a full regression pass on the first build, confirmation testing on every fix, regression around whatever changed, then a release-candidate pass and sign-off.

And one rule was never broken: whoever fixes a bug never gets to close it.

Coding agents skip almost all of that. So I built enhance-qa, a QA team inside your coding agent:

→ A scout maps every screen and control and writes the test checklist
→ Testers run black-box and exploratory tests like real users, with evidence for every bug
→ A fresh verifier reproduces every bug before it's filed, then does confirmation testing on every fix
→ A fixer makes one commit per bug, starting from a failing test
→ A lead runs the pass and gives you a straight go/no-go

Only the fixer touches your code. Nobody grades their own work.

It also keeps the build-by-build rhythm. A qa/ record lives in your repo, so each new build gets a smoke test, fix verification and regression testing scoped to what changed (halo testing). Before you ship, a release pass runs full regression and ends in a go/no-go report.

It tests web apps, iOS and Android, desktop apps, CLIs, APIs, browser extensions, bots, games and AI features.

Bugs only, never feature wishes. It asks before touching data, auth or payments, and never pushes or deploys.

Works with Claude Code and Codex, plus Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and Antigravity.

Free and open source:
http://github.com/rohanvijaykumar/enhance-qa

items.title: Community highlights Claude Code /ship and steward PR repair loops
facts: /code-review before the PR. add --fix and it repairs what it finds.
/ship when the change is done. opens the PR, reviews it, then keeps watching.
/steward 41 for a PR that already exists. starts the watch, skips the opening review.

x_posts.author: @Klarsynx
x_posts.text:
HOLY F*CK. YOUR PR IS NOT THE FINISH LINE. IT'S WHERE CLAUDE CODE STARTS WORKING.

most devs open a pull request and walk away

then CI goes red. a reviewer drops six comments. the branch sits for a week and rots

claude code has a whole workflow for the part everyone skips, and almost nobody uses it

4 COMMANDS. 1 REPAIR LOOP. ONE HUMAN MERGE GATE.

→ /code-review before the PR. add --fix and it repairs what it finds
→ /ship when the change is done. opens the PR, reviews it, then keeps watching
→ /steward 41 for a PR that already exists. starts the watch, skips the opening review
→ /ship stop ends it. /tasks shows what's still running

THE WATCH IS A LOOP, NOT A PROMISE

review → watch CI and comments → small patch → fresh evidence → back to watching

every new push, every new check, every new comment restarts the loop

and it never merges for you. when it's ready, the decision goes to your repo rules and a human

next action ∈ { inspect, patch, verify, wait, escalate }

THE GUARDRAILS THAT MAKE IT SAFE

→ redesigns, scope creep and security questions go straight back to the author
→ three pushes on one issue, then a human takes over
→ up to seven days per watch, then it stops and tells you why

BEFORE YOU WALK AWAY

→ github cli signed in, branch checked out, next task in a separate worktree
→ machine awake, session open. watches spend your quota
→ on native windows the PR still opens, but the local watch won't start

NOW THE PART THAT ACTUALLY COMPOUNDS: STOP FIXING THE SAME BUG TWICE

5 FILES. EACH ONE HAS EXACTLY ONE READER.

→ CLAUDE.md: shared conventions. claude code and local review read it
→ REVIEW.md: severity and exclusions. only managed review reads it, /code-review doesn't
→ skills/verify: how to actually run and check the change
→ skills/steward: house rules for keeping a PR alive
→ approvals.yml: who signs off on which paths. read from the default branch, so a PR can't approve its own policy

THE RULE FOR WRITING RULES:

rule = repeated friction +…
